name: Spinal Cord Tracts and Incomplete Cord Syndromes

reference.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students / Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy
clinicalPearls: Adult spinal cord terminates at lower border of L1 (conus medullaris); dural sac terminates at S2; safe lumbar puncture is L3-L4 or L4-L5
Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) convey proprioception and vibration; ascend uncrossed, decussate in medulla
Lateral spinothalamic tract decussates in anterior white commissure within 1-2 segments, conveying pain and temperature contralaterally
Brown-Sequard syndrome (cord hemisection): ipsilateral spastic paralysis and dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss 1-2 levels below
Syringomyelia causes cape-like bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to central canal cavitation interrupting crossing commissural fibres
reference.pathophysiology: Incomplete cord syndromes result from vascular compromise, trauma or intrinsic cavitation. Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares dorsal columns while infarcting bilateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts. Central cord syndrome (hyperextension injury in cervical spondylosis) impairs upper extremities more than lower extremities because cervical motor fibres lie medially in the lateral corticospinal tract.
additionalDifferentials: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (Vitamin B12 deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Sagittal and axial T2-weighted MRI of spine for cord compression, syrinx or edema
Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP) assessing dorsal column conduction
Motor evoked potentials (MEP) assessing corticospinal integrity
